sections.title: Balaam's First Oracle
observations: In this section, we see Balaam, a non-Israelite prophet, summoned by Balak, the king of Moab, to curse Israel. Balaam's initial response is to seek the Lord's guidance, demonstrating a recognition of God's authority.
God instructs Balaam not to curse Israel because they are blessed. This highlights the theme of God's sovereignty over His people and His promises to them.

sections.title: Balaam's Second Oracle
observations: Balak, frustrated by Balaam's first oracle, takes him to a different location to see if he can curse Israel from there. Balaam again seeks the Lord, showing his dependence on divine revelation.
God reaffirms that Israel is blessed, and Balaam's response is to bless Israel instead of cursing them. This reinforces the idea that God's plans cannot be thwarted by human intentions.

sections.title: Balaam's Third Oracle
observations: In this section, Balak takes Balaam to yet another location, hoping to find a way to curse Israel. Balaam's oracles continue to emphasize Israel's strength and God's favor upon them.
Balaam's declarations about Israel's future victories and blessings serve as a reminder of God's faithfulness to His covenant people.

importantVerses.commentary: How can I curse whom God has not cursed? This verse emphasizes the futility of opposing God's will and the assurance of His blessings upon His people.
Behold, I received a command to bless; He has blessed, and I cannot reverse it. This verse highlights the unchangeable nature of God's blessings and the authority of His word.

questions: What does Balaam's interaction with God teach us about seeking divine guidance?
How does this chapter illustrate the theme of God's sovereignty over nations and individuals?
What implications does Balaam's inability to curse Israel have for understanding God's promises to His people?
